title: Judge the Judge: Building LLM Evaluators That Actually Work with GEPA — Mahmoud Mabrouk, Agenta AI

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

summary:
Mahmoud Mabrouk, co-founder and CEO of Agenta (an open-source LLMOps platform), presents a hands-on workshop on building calibrated LLM-as-a-judge evaluators using GEPA prompt optimization. He argues that miscalibrated judges give false confidence and are worse than no evaluation at all, while calibrated judges accelerate offline iteration loops, enable reliable online monitoring, and support a data flywheel for continuous improvement.

The workshop demonstrates a four-step workflow on τBench's airline customer support benchmark (599 annotated traces, 62%/38% compliant/non-compliant split): design metrics, annotate data, optimize the judge with GEPA, and validate results. Metrics must derive from business use cases via SME error analysis rather than generic measures like hallucination, and should be binary (compliant/non-compliant with reasoning) rather than 1–5 scores. Annotation reasoning is critical because GEPA's optimization uses it to understand why judgments fail.

GEPA works as a genetic algorithm: starting with a seed prompt, it iteratively samples new candidates via mutation (LLM reflects on failures and proposes improvements) and merging (combines guidelines from multiple prompts), evaluates against annotated data batches, and filters using a Pareto frontier that selects the best candidate per task. The workshop uses GEPA's optimize_anything API with a seed candidate, an evaluator function logging diagnostics, and configuration parameters.

In the Jupyter notebook demo, data is split into 480 training and 112 validation traces by task. The seed judge defaults to compliance to prevent random LLM biases, achieving 61% accuracy on validation with 98% compliant predictions. A custom reflection template provides airline domain context and outperforms GEPA's default. After ~1 hour of optimization (~200–300 iterations, ~$200–300 in tokens), validation accuracy improved ~14 points, compliance bias dropped from 98% to 64%, and the Pareto frontier reached 100% per-task accuracy, though merging all winning candidates into a single prompt remains a challenge.

Lessons include: smaller/older models (GPT-4o) fail as judges or refiners; best results used Gemini for reflection and Grok for judge; seed prompts without policy access outperformed those with policy access (likely avoiding local minima); debugging requires small iterations, trace instrumentation, and prompt inspection before scaling; and a bigger model should be used for refinement with a smaller one for the judge, especially for online evaluation at scale.
whyItMatters: The concepts in this workshop form a cohesive engineering methodology for building trustworthy LLM evaluation systems. The four-step workflow (design metrics, annotate, optimize, validate) provides the overarching process, while binary classification metrics and annotation reasoning ensure the optimization target is well-defined and learnable by GEPA. GEPA's genetic algorithm—mutation, merging, and Pareto frontier selection—provides the optimization engine, but its effectiveness depends on critical engineering choices: seed prompt design (defaulting to compliance to avoid random LLM biases), custom reflection templates (providing domain context for complex policy rules), and model selection (bigger for refinement, smaller for judge). The methodology is grounded in a real benchmark (τBench's airline domain) and supported by practical engineering concerns: train/validation splits by task to measure generalization, trace instrumentation for debugging, cost management for sustainable experiments, and the offline/online evaluation distinction for deployment. Together, these concepts address the core challenge of LLM evaluation: building judges that are not just plausible but genuinely calibrated against human judgment, enabling reliable iteration loops and production monitoring without the false confidence that miscalibrated judges create.
temporalContext: The workshop was published in April 2026, when GEPA had been accepted at ICLR 2026 and τBench had already evolved to τ³-bench (June 2025) with additional domains beyond airline and retail. Agenta had open-sourced all evaluation features under MIT license in November 2025. The optimization methodology and tooling described represent the state of the art as of early-to-mid 2026, though GEPA's rapid iteration means the library API may have evolved since the workshop recording.

concepts.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
concepts.explanation: Using an LLM to evaluate the outputs of another LLM system (e.g., a customer support agent) by classifying responses as compliant or non-compliant with reasoning. The core paradigm of the workshop.
concepts.importance: Enables scalable automated evaluation of LLM applications, but miscalibrated judges give false confidence and are worse than no evaluation at all.

concepts.name: GEPA Prompt Optimization
concepts.explanation: An open-source prompt optimization framework (developed at UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab) that uses a genetic-algorithm-style approach to iteratively improve prompts via LLM reflection, mutation, merging, and Pareto frontier selection.
concepts.importance: Provides an automated way to optimize LLM-as-a-judge prompts that manual prompt engineering cannot achieve, especially for complex policy-adherence criteria.

concepts.name: Genetic Algorithm for Prompt Evolution
concepts.explanation: GEPA's core mechanism: start with a seed prompt, iteratively sample new candidates via mutation (LLM reflects on failures and proposes improvements) and merging (combines guidelines from multiple prompts), evaluate against annotated data batches, and filter survivors.
concepts.importance: The genetic approach enables exploration of the prompt space beyond what manual design can reach, discovering policy rules the human designer may not have articulated.

concepts.name: Pareto Frontier Selection
concepts.explanation: GEPA's candidate filtering strategy that selects the best candidate per task/trajectory rather than by average score, promoting diversity and ensuring full test-case coverage across the Pareto frontier.
concepts.importance: Prevents a single high-average-score candidate from dominating while failing on specific tasks; ensures every task has a winning candidate, though merging them into one prompt remains a challenge.

concepts.name: Calibration with Human Annotation
concepts.explanation: Aligning LLM judge outputs with human-labeled ground truth by annotating conversation traces with binary labels (compliant/non-compliant) and reasoning, then optimizing the judge prompt to match human judgment.
concepts.importance: Without calibration, LLM judges introduce systematic biases (e.g., defaulting to compliant 98% of the time) that make evaluation results unreliable for decision-making.

concepts.name: Default-to-Compliance Bias
concepts.explanation: An LLM judge's tendency to predict 'compliant' by default (98% in the seed judge), which must be explicitly counteracted by designing the seed prompt to default to compliance deliberately so the optimizer can learn to identify non-compliance.
concepts.importance: Without an explicit default bias direction, the LLM applies random biases that are very hard to correct during optimization; a deliberate starting bias gives the optimizer a productive correction target.

concepts.name: Local Minima in Prompt Optimization
concepts.explanation: Seed prompts with access to the agent's policy can trap GEPA's optimization in a local minimum, while seeds without policy access outperform because the optimizer can discover rules more freely.
concepts.importance: Understanding optimization landscape dynamics is critical for seed design; providing too much information upfront can paradoxically limit the optimizer's ability to find better solutions.

concepts.name: Model Selection for Judge vs Refiner
concepts.explanation: Using different model sizes and families for different roles in GEPA optimization: a bigger model for the refinement/reflection step and a smaller model for the judge, especially for cost-sensitive online evaluation. GPT-4o failed completely; best results used Gemini for reflection and Grok for judge.
concepts.importance: Model choice dramatically affects optimization outcomes; smaller/older models cannot handle complex policy logic, but using the largest model everywhere is cost-prohibitive for production evaluation.

concepts.name: τBench Benchmark
concepts.explanation: A benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in real-world domains, created by Sierra, featuring an airline customer support domain with conversation traces for evaluating agent compliance with domain-specific policies. Accepted at ICLR 2025.
concepts.importance: Provides a realistic, complex evaluation scenario with policy constraints, annotation ground truth, and enough traces to train and validate LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.

concepts.name: Annotation Reasoning for Optimization
concepts.explanation: Providing textual reasoning alongside binary labels during annotation, which GEPA's optimization algorithm uses to understand why judgments fail and to propose targeted prompt improvements.
concepts.importance: Without reasoning, the optimizer must discover failure causes itself, which is much harder and less effective; reasoning transforms annotations from labels into learnable optimization signals.

concepts.name: Data Flywheel for Continuous Improvement
concepts.explanation: A system design where calibrated evaluation enables a data flywheel: better judges produce better labeled data, which improves agents, which generates more data for further calibration and improvement.
concepts.importance: Without calibrated evaluation, the flywheel breaks—miscalibrated judges introduce noise that compounds through iterations, degrading rather than improving the system over time.

concepts.name: Actionable Side Information (ASI)
concepts.explanation: GEPA's term for the diagnostic feedback that evaluator functions log (output, error, reasoning) to guide the mutation and reflection loop. The transcript describes this as 'logging diagnostics' without using the ASI term.
concepts.importance: ASI is the mechanism by which GEPA's optimizer learns from execution traces; rich diagnostics enable targeted mutations rather than random perturbations.

concepts.name: Evaluation Pipeline Architecture
concepts.explanation: A systematic four-step engineering process for building calibrated LLM evaluators: design metrics from use-case error analysis, annotate data with reasoning, optimize the judge prompt with GEPA, and validate results against held-out data.
concepts.importance: Provides a repeatable, structured methodology for building reliable evaluation systems instead of ad-hoc judge construction, ensuring judges are calibrated before deployment.

concepts.name: Binary Classification Metrics for Evaluation
concepts.explanation: Binary compliant/non-compliant metrics with reasoning are preferred over 1–5 scores because even binary calibration is hard, and inter-annotator agreement on scales is poor.
concepts.importance: Simplifies calibration, improves annotator consistency, and makes optimization targets well-defined for GEPA's genetic algorithm.

concepts.name: Train/Validation Split by Task
concepts.explanation: Splitting annotated data by task into 480 training and 112 validation traces with no cross-set redundancy, ensuring the validation set measures generalization rather than memorization of identical task instances.
concepts.importance: Prevents inflated validation scores from repeated task instances appearing in both sets, which would mislead optimization assessment.

concepts.name: Trace Instrumentation for Debugging
concepts.explanation: Instrumenting optimization traces in Agenta to inspect generated prompts, reasoning, and evaluation failures during GEPA debugging, enabling root-cause analysis of optimization failures.
concepts.importance: Without trace-level visibility, debugging prompt optimization is guesswork; instrumented traces let developers identify whether failures stem from bad seeds, wrong models, or insufficient iterations.

concepts.name: Cost Management for Optimization Experiments
concepts.explanation: Optimization experiments cost ~$200–300 in tokens due to long trajectories and many iterations; strategic model selection (bigger model for refinement, smaller for judge) manages costs, especially for online evaluation at scale.
concepts.importance: Without cost planning, optimization experiments can become prohibitively expensive; understanding cost drivers enables sustainable evaluation pipelines.

concepts.name: Seed Prompt Engineering
concepts.explanation: Designing an initial seed judge prompt that defaults to a known bias direction (compliance) to prevent random LLM biases that are very hard to correct during optimization. Seed prompt quality significantly impacts whether optimization can learn at all.
concepts.importance: A well-designed seed gives the optimizer a productive starting point; a near-random seed may fail to learn entirely, making this the most critical engineering decision in the pipeline.

concepts.name: Custom Reflection Template Design
concepts.explanation: Writing domain-specific reflection templates for GEPA that provide domain context (airline customer service) and instruct the LLM to discover policy rules, outperforming GEPA's generic default template for complex policy-adherence use cases.
concepts.importance: Generic templates lack domain context needed for complex evaluation criteria; custom templates enable the optimizer to discover relevant rules rather than making generic improvements.

concepts.name: Offline vs Online Evaluation Architecture
concepts.explanation: Distinguishing between offline evaluation (iterating during development with larger models) and online evaluation (monitoring in production with smaller, cost-efficient models), with different model size and cost trade-offs for each.
concepts.importance: Offline evaluation accelerates development iteration; online evaluation requires cost-efficient judges for continuous monitoring at scale, and the architecture must account for both.

concepts.name: Iterative Debugging Methodology
concepts.explanation: A debugging strategy of starting with small iterations, examining reasoning and generated candidates, instrumenting traces, and overfitting to training data before scaling up to full experiments.
concepts.importance: Scaling up prematurely wastes compute and obscures root causes; small-scale debugging identifies fundamental issues cheaply before committing to expensive full optimization runs.

concepts.name: Error Analysis and Metric Design
concepts.explanation: Deriving evaluation metrics from SME error analysis of actual conversation traces rather than using generic measures like hallucination. Annotation revealed four error types: policy adherence, response style, information delivery, and tool calling, each requiring a separate judge.
concepts.importance: Use-case-specific metrics ensure the evaluation measures what matters for the business; generic metrics like hallucination may miss the actual failure modes that degrade customer experience.

sections.title: Motivation: Why Calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge Matters
sections.summary: Opens with a scenario where a naive hallucination judge is deployed in production monitoring but fails to detect real problems. Introduces the goal: building LLM-as-a-judge evaluators calibrated with human annotations using GEPA prompt optimization. Explains three motivations: faster offline evaluation loops, reliable online evaluation, and enabling a data flywheel for continuous automatic improvement.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Agenta
sections.summary: Mahmoud Mabrouk introduces himself as co-founder and CEO of Agenta, an open-source LLMOps platform covering observability, prompt management, and evaluation. He has 15+ years in ML, previously in academia working on computational biology and protein structure prediction.

sections.title: Workshop Plan and Dataset
sections.summary: Outlines the practical use case: a customer support agent evaluated via τBench (built by Sierra). The airline agent benchmark includes 599 conversation traces with human annotations. Data is 62% compliant / 38% non-compliant, generated across multiple models. The dataset is complex but somewhat noisy, making it a good real-world test for GEPA.

sections.title: Four-Step Workflow and Metric Design
sections.summary: Describes the four-step workflow: design metrics, annotate data, optimize the judge, validate. Emphasizes metrics must come from the use case via SME error analysis (referencing Hamel's guide). Shows how annotating traces revealed four error types—policy adherence, response style, information delivery, tool calling—and explains the plan to build four separate judges rather than one monolithic judge, since even simplified judges are hard to calibrate.

sections.title: Binary Metrics and Annotation with Reasoning
sections.summary: Explains metrics should be binary (compliant/non-compliant) rather than 1–5 scores because even binary calibration is hard and inter-annotator agreement on scales is poor. Demonstrates annotation in Agenta: creating annotation queues where annotators provide binary labels plus reasoning. The reasoning is critical for GEPA—without it, the optimization algorithm cannot discover why judgments fail. Notes that data preparation and annotation are the hardest parts, and acknowledges τBench data limitations.

sections.title: GEPA Algorithm: How It Works
sections.summary: Explains GEPA as a genetic-algorithm-style optimizer: start with a seed prompt, iteratively sample new candidates using mutation (LLM reflects on failures and proposes improvements) and merging (combines guidelines from multiple prompts), evaluate against batches of annotated data, and filter using a Pareto frontier. The Pareto frontier selects the best candidate per task/trajectory rather than by average score, promoting diversity and ensuring full test-case coverage. The loop continues until the compute budget is exhausted.

sections.title: GEPA Library and Optimize Anything API
sections.summary: Introduces the GEPA open-source library and its new 'optimize anything' API. The API takes a seed candidate (prompt, dict, or chain of prompts), an evaluator function that runs the system and logs diagnostics (output, error, reasoning), and configuration parameters like calls per iteration and refinement prompt context. The evaluator's logged diagnostics feed back into the mutation/reflection loop. Mahmoud emphasizes understanding the algorithm internals is essential for effective parameter tuning.

sections.title: Jupyter Notebook: Data Loading, Split, and Seed Judge Design
sections.summary: Walks through the Jupyter notebook: installing flight_lm and gepa libraries, loading preprocessed τBench data, and splitting into 480 training traces and 112 validation traces by task with no cross-set redundancy. Shows example annotations with reasoning explaining compliant vs non-compliant verdicts. Designs a seed judge that explicitly defaults to compliance—without this, the LLM applies its own random biases and is very hard to optimize. The seed judge achieves 61% accuracy on validation, predicting compliant 98% of the time, which is the desired starting bias. Mahmoud notes the seed prompt quality is critical: experiments with near-random seeds failed to learn at all.

sections.title: Custom Reflection Template and Optimization Results
sections.summary: Details the custom reflection template written for GEPA instead of the default, providing airline customer service domain context and instructing the LLM to discover real policy rules. The default template did not understand it should learn the policy. The run_optimization wrapper parameterizes optimize_anything for repeated experiments. After ~1 hour of optimization, the rubric learned policy criteria for flight cancellation, modification, and communication. Validation accuracy improved ~14 points; training accuracy improved 9 points. Compliance bias dropped from 98% to 64%, and non-compliant recall/precision rose from zero. The Pareto frontier achieved 100% per-task accuracy, but merging all winning candidates into a single unified prompt remained the algorithm's core challenge.

sections.title: Lessons Learned: Model Selection, Debugging, Seed Prompts, and Cost
sections.summary: Mahmoud shares lessons from failed experiments. The optimized judge improved but remains far from 95% accuracy or strong human alignment. Smaller/older models (e.g., GPT-4o) failed completely as judges and refiners for complex policy logic. Best results used Gemini for reflection and Grok for judge; GPT-4 mini for both also worked well. Debugging strategy: start with small iterations, examine reasoning and generated candidates, instrument traces in Agenta, and overfit to training data before scaling up. Seed prompts without access to the agent's policy outperformed those with policy access, likely because policy access traps optimization in a local minimum. Experiments cost ~$200–300 in tokens due to long trajectories; GPT-4 was too expensive to sustain. He recommends a bigger model for refinement and a smaller one for the judge, especially for online evaluation at scale, and notes ~200–300 iterations per experiment plus batch-size and other parameter tuning are needed.

organization.name: Agenta
organization.summary: Agenta is an open-source platform (MIT licensed) founded in 2023 in Berlin, Germany, with approximately 5 employees and ~$1.2M in total funding. Co-founded by Mahmoud Mabrouk (CEO), the company has evolved from an LLMOps platform (v1.0) focused on prompt management, evaluation, and observability to an agent workspace (v2.0) for building, running, and sharing AI agents. At the time of the video (April 2026), Agenta was in its LLMOps platform phase. As of November 2025, all functional features including evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge, test sets, custom evaluators), prompt management, and observability were open-sourced under MIT license. The platform retains these evaluation, observability, and prompt management capabilities used in the workshop for trace annotation, error clustering, and debugging during GEPA optimization.
organization.status: Active — Agenta 2.0 launched as an open-source agent workspace; all functional features remain MIT-licensed

technologies.label: GEPA Prompt Optimization Framework
technologies.summary: GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) is an open-source prompt optimization framework developed at UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab that uses a genetic-algorithm-style approach to iteratively improve prompts via LLM-guided reflection, mutation, and merging, filtering candidates using Pareto frontier selection. The workshop demonstrates GEPA's optimize_anything API to optimize LLM-as-a-judge evaluator prompts on the τBench airline dataset, achieving ~14 point validation accuracy improvement, reducing compliance bias from 98% to 64%, and reaching 100% per-task accuracy on the Pareto frontier after ~1 hour of optimization (~200-300 iterations, ~$200-300 in tokens). Key lessons include the need for custom reflection templates over GEPA defaults for complex policy logic, strategic model selection (bigger for refinement, smaller for judge), and careful seed prompt design without policy access to avoid local minima.
technologies.role: Core technology demonstrated hands-on - the workshop shows GEPA's optimize_anything API with seed candidates, evaluator functions, configuration parameters, custom reflection templates, and detailed result analysis including accuracy, bias reduction, and Pareto frontier coverage

technologies.label: LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
technologies.summary: LLM-as-a-Judge is an evaluation paradigm where an LLM evaluates the outputs of another LLM system by classifying responses as compliant or non-compliant with reasoning. The workshop teaches a four-step workflow to build calibrated judges: design use-case-specific metrics via SME error analysis, annotate data with reasoning, optimize the judge with GEPA, and validate results. The presenter argues miscalibrated judges give false confidence and are worse than no evaluation at all, while calibrated judges enable faster offline iteration loops, reliable online monitoring, and a data flywheel for continuous improvement. Metrics must be binary rather than 1-5 scales, and annotation reasoning is critical for GEPA optimization to learn from failures. Even after optimization, the judge remained far from 95% accuracy or strong human alignment, highlighting calibration as an ongoing challenge.
technologies.role: Central topic - the entire workshop is about building calibrated LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, covering metric design from SME error analysis, annotation with reasoning, optimization with GEPA, and validation against held-out data

technologies.label: τBench Benchmark
technologies.summary: τBench is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in real-world domains, created by Sierra and accepted at ICLR 2025. The airline customer support domain provides 599 annotated conversation traces (62% compliant, 38% non-compliant) used in the workshop as the practical dataset for building and optimizing LLM-as-a-judge evaluators. The benchmark features domain-specific API tools, policy guidelines, and ground truth annotations for customer service scenarios involving flight booking, modification, cancellation, and refunds. It has since evolved to τ³-bench with additional domains (retail, telecom, banking_knowledge) and voice evaluation, with audited and fixed airline tasks.
technologies.role: Practical use case dataset - provides the 599 airline customer support traces used to demonstrate the four-step evaluation workflow, including the 480/112 train-validation split by task

technologies.label: Agenta Platform
technologies.summary: Agenta is an open-source platform (MIT licensed) for building and running AI agents, co-founded by the workshop presenter Mahmoud Mabrouk and based in Berlin. It provides annotation queues with reasoning, error clustering, trace instrumentation, and observability features used throughout the workshop for data preparation, debugging during GEPA optimization, and examining generated prompts and reasoning. The platform has evolved from an LLMOps platform (v1.0) to an agent workspace (v2.0) while retaining evaluation, observability, and prompt management capabilities. All functional features were open-sourced under MIT license in November 2025.

entities.relation: Creator of the τBench benchmark used in the workshop. Sierra built τBench to measure how well AI agents converse with users, call tools, retrieve knowledge, and follow policy across enterprise domains.

entities.name: UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab
entities.relation: Research lab associated with GEPA, the prompt optimization library demonstrated in the workshop. GEPA is listed as a project on the Sky Computing Lab website, providing institutional backing.

resources.title: Agenta — The open-source workspace for your agents
resources.why: Agenta is a real open-source platform for building and running AI agents, MIT-licensed and self-hostable, based in Berlin.

resources.title: What is Agenta? - Docs
resources.why: Fetched and verified. Current v2.0 describes Agenta as 'a workspace where you and your team build agents and automations.' Features include tracing/usage inspection, version history, and MIT-licensed self-hosting. The platform has evolved from an LLMOps platform (v1.0) to an agent workspace (v2.0), but retains evaluation, observability, and prompt management capabilities.

resources.title: Agenta-AI/agenta: The open-source LLMOps platform
resources.why: Confirms Agenta is a real open-source platform. GitHub description matches: 'prompt playground, prompt management, LLM evaluation, and LLM observability all in one place.' MIT licensed. Mahmoud Mabrouk (mmabrouk) is the top contributor with 5807 contributions.

resources.title: Launch Week #2 Day 4: Open Sourcing Evaluation
resources.why: Confirms that as of November 2025, Agenta open-sourced all functional features under MIT license, including evaluation (LLM-as-a-judge, test sets, custom evaluators), prompt management, and observability. This validates the transcript's description of Agenta as an open-source LLMOps platform with these features. Published 2025-11-13, before the video's April 2026 publication.

resources.title: agenta v0.36.2 on PyPI
resources.why: Confirms Mahmoud Mabrouk is the author (mahmoud@agenta.ai). Package description: 'The SDK for agenta is an open-source LLMOps platform' with 'Prompt playground, prompt management, evaluation, and observability.' This matches the transcript's description of Agenta.

resources.title: Mahmoud Mabrouk - GitHub Profile
resources.why: Confirms Mahmoud Mabrouk is 'Cofounder of @Agenta-AI', located in Berlin, with blog at agenta.ai. Has 62 public repos and 304 followers. This verifies his role as co-founder of Agenta as stated in the transcript.

resources.title: GEPA: Optimize prompts, code, and more with AI-powered Reflective Text Evolution
resources.why: Official repository confirming GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) is a real framework for optimizing any system with textual parameters. README describes the iterative reflection, mutation, and Pareto-aware selection algorithm matching the transcript's description of mutation, merging, and Pareto frontier.

resources.title: GEPA: Optimize Anything with LLMs
resources.why: Confirms GEPA uses LLMs to read full execution traces and diagnose failures via Actionable Side Information (ASI), matching the transcript's description of GEPA's reflection-based optimization. Notes rapid optimization in minutes to hours via API access.

resources.title: Quick Start - GEPA
resources.why: Fetched and verified: the optimize_anything API accepts a seed_candidate, an evaluator function that logs diagnostics (ASI), an objective description, and a GEPAConfig. This matches the transcript's description of the API taking seed candidates, evaluator functions, and configuration parameters. Also shows DSPy integration as Option 3.

resources.title: API Overview - GEPA
resources.why: Documents the full API surface including optimize_anything, GEPAAdapter, Proposers (ReflectiveMutationProposer, MergeProposer), and Strategies (ParetoCandidateSelector, BatchSampler). This matches the transcript's mentions of mutation, merging, Pareto frontier, and batch evaluation.

resources.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
resources.why: Confirms GEPA is a real, peer-reviewed optimizer. Authored by Lakshya Agrawal, Shangyin Tan, Omar Khattab, Matei Zaharia, Dan Klein, Ion Stoica, and others. Paper claims GEPA outperforms GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20% while using up to 35x fewer rollouts. Also outperforms MIPROv2 by over 10%.

resources.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning (ICLR 2026)
resources.why: Confirms GEPA paper was accepted at ICLR 2026, establishing its academic credibility. The paper formalizes the GEPA algorithm with genetic prompt evolution, reflection using natural language feedback, and Pareto-based candidate selection.

resources.title: GEPA - UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab
resources.why: Confirms GEPA is associated with UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab, providing institutional credibility. Describes GEPA as optimizing arbitrary systems composed of text components against any evaluation metric.

resources.title: UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab
resources.why: UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab is a real research lab that hosts GEPA as an official project.

resources.title: Better customer experiences | Sierra
resources.why: Sierra is a real conversational AI platform company for businesses, headquartered in San Francisco.

resources.title: About Sierra
resources.why: Sierra was co-founded by Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, who first met while working together at Google.

resources.title: τ-Bench: Benchmarking AI agents for the real-world - Sierra Blog
resources.why: First-party confirmation from Sierra that they built τBench. Describes the benchmark as measuring an agent's ability to interact with simulated human users and programmatic APIs while following domain-specific policies. Confirms airline and retail domains. Published 2024-06-20.

resources.title: τ-bench — Benchmarking AI Agents on Real-World Tasks
resources.why: Confirms the benchmark is actively maintained with leaderboards. Shows evolution to τ³-bench with voice evaluation and banking knowledge domain. The airline domain is confirmed as a core domain. The pass^k reliability metric is used for scoring.

resources.title: sierra-research/tau-bench: Code and Data for Tau-Bench
resources.why: Fetched and verified. Confirms τBench is a real benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a simulated user and a language agent with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. Includes airline and retail domains. MIT licensed. 1.4k stars. Now superseded by τ³-bench but the airline domain data remains available. Includes historical trajectories for the airline environment.

resources.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
resources.why: Confirms τBench is authored by Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, and Karthik Narasimhan. The airline domain involves booking, modifying, or canceling flight reservations with 300 flights between 20 US cities and complex policy constraints. This matches the transcript's description of the airline customer support benchmark.

resources.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains (ICLR 2025)
resources.why: Confirms τBench was accepted at ICLR 2025, establishing its academic credibility. The paper describes the benchmark's modular framework with realistic databases/APIs, domain-specific policy documents, and ground truth annotations for customer service scenarios.

resources.title: sierra-research/tau2-bench (τ³-bench)
resources.why: Confirms τBench has evolved to τ²-bench/τ³-bench with additional domains (airline, retail, telecom, banking_knowledge) and voice evaluation. Shows the benchmark is actively maintained. Published 2025-06-09. The airline domain from the original τBench remains available with audited and fixed tasks.

evidence.excerpt: the metrics need to come from uh the use case itself. it does not make sense to have general metrics like hallucination
evidence.supports: Metrics must be use-case-specific, not generic like hallucination

evidence.excerpt: move away from one to five scores or like percentages and instead have like really binary solution
evidence.supports: Binary metrics preferred over 1-5 scores for easier calibration

evidence.excerpt: the reasoning here is very important because without the reasoning we will see the optimization algorithm will need to discover itself like why it failed
evidence.supports: Annotation reasoning is essential for GEPA optimization to learn from failures

evidence.excerpt: you should start by assuming that the agent is compliant and uh only change to non-compliant if there is a specific reason
evidence.supports: Seed judge should default to compliance to avoid random LLM biases

evidence.excerpt: I did not use their default but actually I wrote one. Uh I tried in the beginning by using the default prompt... but the results were not as good as I expected
evidence.supports: Custom reflection template outperformed GEPA's default for complex policy-adherence use case

evidence.excerpt: the LLM as a judge is uh has less bias at 64%. So previously it was 98%
evidence.supports: Compliance bias reduced from 98% to 64% after optimization

evidence.excerpt: the parto frontier interestingly accuracy is now 100%. Meaning that for each task there is one candidate that we generated that solved it
evidence.supports: Pareto frontier achieved 100% per-task accuracy, but merging into one prompt is the challenge

evidence.excerpt: it's very still quite far from kind of 95% accuracy or something that is really well aligned with the human judgment
evidence.supports: Optimized judge still far from 95% accuracy or strong human alignment

evidence.excerpt: using GPD40 for both the refiner and the LLM as a judge and that was a complete failure like uh smaller models really are very bad
evidence.supports: Smaller/older models fail completely as judges or refiners for complex use cases

evidence.excerpt: the uh prompt that did not have access to the policy did uh better because my hypothesis is that if you have access to the agent policy from the beginning then it's very hard to fine-tune it. You're already stuck in a local minima
evidence.supports: Seed prompts without agent policy access outperform those with policy access by avoiding local minima

evidence.excerpt: beware of the cost. I mean um even these small experiments I've done I think they cost like $2 $300
you should use uh kind of a bigger model for the refinement prompt and smaller model for the LLM as a judge
evidence.supports: Use bigger model for refinement, smaller model for judge, especially for online evaluation
